theme: Three cafe formats: guest segments, service, staffing, regulars, starting profiles (build/FORMATS.md, task A1 of round 3)
howNumbersWereChecked: No new web search. Every number is taken from the fragments D02, D05, D06 and D14 on branch claude/jolly-volta-dv0cll (their source and confidence are repeated here) or is an estimate with its arithmetic in the note. 'verified' is used only where the fragment's author opened the page or computed the number from open data. The examples in build/FORMATS.md are computed by packs/parts/cafe/D20-examples.mjs from this file, packs/cafe.json and data/places.json.

guestSegments.note: Four groups of guests. D06 has five; remote workers with laptops are folded into residents (see residents.note). Shares by block are D06 planning values: nobody publishes this split. The shifts are deviations from the average customer the engine already models (footfall.priceSensitivity 2.7; quality 0.93 and reputation 0.74 per unit), so a shop at the reference price with quality 0.5, the reference room and no walk-aways gets a fit of exactly 1. priceShift rule: each group's shift is set so that the price that earns most from that group alone sits at the group's ticket in D06 (commuters $6.50, residents $9, students $6, tourists $12). With a marginal cost of about $4.90 an order (goods $2.21, cups and card fees $0.50, labor $2.20) the best price is e / (e - 1) x 4.90, where e is the group's sensitivity x 0.75 (the share of the block's buyers a shop does not already hold). D06 bounds a cafe's elasticity between 1.3 and 4.7; the cap is used for students.

segments.name: Office commuters
segments.note: sitShare 0.1: D06 seatUse. week and months: D06 office profiles (Placer.ai share of weekday office visits 2025: Tue 24.3%, Wed 23.7%, Thu 21.8%, Fri 12.4%). morningShare 0.55 is set so that an office block (60% commuters) has 44% of its orders between 7 and 10 am, the sum of the D06 office hour curve 0.12 + 0.18 + 0.14: 0.6 x 0.55 + 0.15 x 0.15 + 0.2 x 0.38 + 0.05 x 0.2 = 0.44. dwellHours 0.25: my estimate, a quarter of an hour at a window stool. priceShift +2.7: ticket $6.50 gives e x 0.75 = 6.5 / (6.5 - 4.9) = 4.06, e = 5.4, shift = 5.4 - 2.7. D06 says commuters pay for speed before 9 am: that is waitPull; over a month they buy about 20 cups, so the price of the cup is the largest line of their coffee budget. qualityShift -1.2: the cup is fuel; cancels the engine's quality term and a third of its reputation term. My estimate. seatPull 0.03: nobody sits. waitPull 2.0: a week in which 10% of customers walked away from the line costs exp(-0.2) = 18% of this group; D06: they leave at more than about five people in line. regularShare 0.55: low end of D06's 55-65% steady share of regulars.

segments.name: Residents and regulars
segments.note: D06 residents (55% of a residential block, seatUse 0.4) plus remote workers with laptops (15%, seatUse 1.0): sitShare = (0.55 x 0.4 + 0.15 x 1.0) / 0.70 = 0.53. dwellHours: D14 gives half an hour for an ordinary visit and one hour with laptops; D06 says a remote worker holds a seat two to four hours. Weighted by seated guests: (0.22 x 0.5 + 0.15 x 1.1) / 0.37 = 0.74, rounded to 0.75. week: D06 neighborhood profile (Toast 2023: Saturday +15%, Friday +9%, Monday -10%). months: D06 neighborhood curve, which follows the subway index computed from MTA data. morningShare 0.38: D06 neighborhood hour curve has 0.36 between 7 and 10 am for the whole block. priceShift +0.4: ticket $9 gives e x 0.75 = 9 / 4.1 = 2.2, e = 2.9, shift +0.2; raised to +0.4 because D06 says they notice every price change. qualityShift -0.4 on a mid block: the engine already pays +40% demand for quality and reputation 0.7; on a mid-rent block part of that is not there. The tier of the block moves both (tierPriceShift, tierQualityShift). seatPull 0.2 (a room of 30 seats against 18 draws +22% of this group; remote workers are in it), waitPull 0.5 (D06: they forgive a line): my estimates. regularShare 0.65: top of D06's 55-65%.

segments.name: Students
segments.note: sitShare 0.8: D06 seatUse. D06: afternoons and evenings, term time only, high price sensitivity, leave if prices rise or seats are gone. dwellHours 1.5: my estimate between an ordinary visit (0.5 h) and D06's two to four hours for a laptop seat. week and months: my estimates from the academic calendar (fall term September to mid-December, spring term late January to mid-May, summer at about half); months average 1. morningShare 0.2: my estimate. priceShift +3.6: ticket $6 would give e = 7.3; capped at the top of D06's range, e x 0.75 = 4.7, e = 6.3, shift = 6.3 - 2.7. qualityShift -1.0: my estimate (a cheap drink and a table). seatPull 0.4: a room of 30 seats against 18 draws exp(0.4) = +49% of this group. regularShare 0.4: my estimate (they leave every summer).

segments.name: Tourists and day visitors
segments.note: sitShare 0.5 and the $12 ticket: D06. D06: low price sensitivity, 10 am to 5 pm, they choose by the map rating and come once. week and months: D06 tourist profiles (estimates). dwellHours 0.5: D14 standard visit. priceShift -1.0: ticket $12 gives e x 0.75 = 12 / 7.1 = 1.69, e = 2.25, shift -0.45; lowered to -1.0 because a one-time visitor has no remembered price to compare with (my estimate). qualityShift +1.2: quality stands in for the map rating, my estimate. regularShare 0.05: they do not come back (D06).

guestSegments.mixNote: D06 extra.guestSegments.mixByBlock with remote workers added to residents. Planning values.

blockRules.note: Weights of the four block types for one place; the guest mix is the weighted average of mixByBlock. residential is always 1. office = min(maxWeight, sum over subway stations within reachM of riders a day / ridersRef x nearness). campus = weight x nearness of the nearest college. tourist = the largest of museum, plaza and park weights x nearness. nearness = 1 - distance / reach, the same shape as the engine's overlap(). Reach distances repeat ANCHOR_REACH_M in shared/src/place.ts where they exist (subway 250, college 400); 200 m for tourist anchors is the park reach. The weights are my estimates, chosen so that the 116 storefronts of the East Village map split into all four types: 67 residential, 10 office, 23 campus, 16 tourist (node packs/parts/cafe/D20-examples.mjs, section A). The map has no true office district: the most commuter-heavy door has 49% commuters.

guestSegments.tierNote: Added to the residents' priceShift and qualityShift: residents of a prime block (rent $326 per sq ft in pack.extra.rentByTier) mind the price less and pay for quality; residents of a cheap block the opposite. My estimates.
guestSegments.seatNote: seatIndex = clamp((seats - refSeats) / seatSpan, -1, 1). 18 is pack.sizing.default; 6 seats (pack.sizing.min) give -1, 30 seats give +1.

service.note: Seats limit only guests who sit; takeaway is limited by the team's speed; the morning rush is where orders are lost. Replaces the engine's seat limit, which divided by (1 - takeaway) and so cut takeaway orders too (D14).
service.rushNote: D14 hourProfile: 12%, 15% and 12% of the day's orders at 7, 8 and 9 am; as shares of the rush: 0.12 / 0.39 = 0.31, 0.15 / 0.39 = 0.38. How much of the day falls into the rush comes from the guests (guestSegments.morningShare), not from here.
service.peak15Note: D14: the busiest quarter-hour carries a third of the hour (commuter waves off the trains). An estimate; traffic engineering uses 0.85-0.95 for cars.
service.machineNote: D14: ceiling of one two-group machine and its grinders, in orders (about 108 drinks at 1.2 drinks an order). D06: 100 drinks an hour is the practical top of a two-group machine. https://www.seattlecoffeegear.com/blogs/scg-blog/drinks-per-hour
service.walkAwayNote: Share of arriving customers who walk on when this many people stand in line; straight lines between the points, 0 below 5, 0.5 above 20. D06 extra.queue.walkAwayByPeopleAhead with the steps joined: up to five people nobody leaves (Lu, Musalem, Olivares, Schilkrut, deli counter study, paper opened by D06); a line of 10 costs like a 3.2% price rise and a line of 15 like 11.5%, which D06 converts to 10% and 30% of buyers. These are shares of the flow, not chances: the day's result is fixed by its inputs.
service.seatPeakNote: Share of a day's seated guests who arrive in the busiest hour: the peak of the D06 neighborhood hour curve (0.14 at 8 am).
service.seatFillNote: Share of seats that can be filled at once: a table for two often holds one guest. My estimate.
service.seatBusyNote: Hours a day a full room stays full. My estimate: the D06 neighborhood curve has three hours at or above 0.10 of the day.
service.noSeatNote: D14: of the guests who find no seat, 60% take the order away and 40% leave. An estimate.
service.sitInLaborNote: Work per seated order against a takeaway order: ceramic, the table, the dishes, the restroom. My estimate: in a cafe where 40% of orders are seated (pack.sizing.takeawayShare 0.6) one person in four works the room, not the bar: seated order = (0.75 + 0.25 / 0.4) / 0.75 = 1.83, rounded to 1.8.
service.crowdNote: The pack's sizing.crowdPenaltyAbove and the engine's 0.08 quality drop, judged by seats in use at the busiest hour, not by the day's average.
service.floorNote: Seats that fit = floor((sqft - fixedCoreSqft) / sqftPerSeat). D02 extra.floorPlan: the fixed core of a counter-service cafe is 395 sq ft (bar 120, line and pickup 70, restroom 60, back of house 120, entry 25) and barely changes with the size of the space; 18 net sq ft a seat is D02's 'comfortable' and pack.sizing.sqftPerUnit. A 500 sq ft door fits 5 seats, 600 fits 11, 830 fits 24. Seats above that number do not exist for the service part.

staffing.note: What a shift lead and an experienced barista give, what a trainee costs, and whether the paid hours cover the open hours.
staffing.rolesNote: D05 skillRamp (reading of Perfect Daily Grind time marks, not measurements): after twelve months a barista works at 1.1 of the trained speed, adds 0.02 to quality, can train others and open alone: that is the shift lead. A new hire works at 0.4 in weeks 1-2, 0.7 in weeks 3-6 and 0.85 in months 2-3, with quality -0.03 to -0.02. Averaged over the first 13 weeks with someone to train them: (2 x 0.4 + 4 x 0.7 + 7 x 0.85) / 13 = 0.73, rounded to 0.75. Without a lead the new hire stays on register and bar-back longer: I take the mean of the first two stages, (0.4 + 0.7) / 2 = 0.55. https://perfectdailygrind.com/2019/08/how-long-should-it-take-you-to-train-your-baristas/
staffing.ordersPerPaidHourNote: Takeaway orders per paid hour of a trained barista, averaged over the month. The pack's 1,700 orders per person a month / 160 hours = 10.6 is for a shop where 40% of orders are seated; with a seated order costing 1.8 of a takeaway order (service.sitInLaborMult) the same team makes 10.625 x (1 + 0.4 x 0.8) = 14.0 takeaway orders an hour. The reference shop keeps its 1,700.
staffing.rushNote: D14 and D06: one barista alone makes about 30 drinks an hour on a two-group machine, 1.2 drinks an order: 25 orders an hour per person on the floor in the rush. https://www.ekuep.com/en/two-groups
staffing.rushCrewNote: People at the bar in the morning rush = rushCrewOwner + rushCrewShare x workers. D14 puts half the team on the rush; the pack counts the owner or the hired manager as a fifth pair of hands (pack.capacity.note).
staffing.leadNote: With three or more workers and no shift lead nobody assigns the stations. speedMult: D05 stations, a two-barista bar makes 35 to 45 drinks an hour; the bottom of the band against its middle is 35 / 40 = 0.875, rounded to 0.9. The two quality numbers are my estimates of the same size as the engine's penalty for a short-staffed day (0.04).
staffing.minOnFloorNote: pack.capacity.minStaff: two people is the legal and practical floor (a Food Protection Certificate holder on site every open hour).
staffing.openHoursNote: By option of the pack lever 'hours': 7am-7pm is 12 hours, 6am-9pm is 15. The long option already costs $2,300 a month in the pack, which is three more hours a day for one person (90 hours at about $25.50 with payroll taxes), so it brings 90 paid hours with it. 'short' (7am-3pm) is a proposed new option: see newLeverOptions.
staffing.ownerHoursNote: pack.extra.referenceMonth prices the owner's 160 hours at $4,800; a hired manager works the same hours.
staffing.uncoveredNote: Hours nobody can cover are cut from the end of the day. D06 neighborhood hour curve: the last four open hours carry 0.07 + 0.06 + 0.05 + 0.05 = 0.23 of the day, 0.0575 an hour against the average 1 / 12 = 0.0833: 0.69.

newRoles.name: New barista (first 90 days)
newRoles.note: D05: 2026 postings start at $17.00 (the legal minimum) and $18.50 plus tips; $18 is the midpoint for a hire with little bar experience. 120 hours is 28 hours a week.

newLeverOptions.note: Closing at 3 pm gives up the hours 3 to 7 pm: 23% of the day on a neighborhood block and 16% on an office block (D06 hour curves); 0.2 is the mean. The saving is in people: 8 open hours need 480 floor hours a month instead of 720.

staffing.leverSpeedNote: Speed of the bar by lever option. Specialty sourcing: D06 gives one minute for an espresso and two for a milk drink; a house menu at half and half is 1.5 minutes a drink, a specialty menu at one quarter and three quarters is 1.75: 1.5 / 1.75 = 0.86, rounded to 0.85. The split of the menus is my estimate.

regulars.note: Regulars are a bonus or a loss on top of the engine's awareness ramp, not a second ramp: a shop with quality 0.5 and reputation 0.5 gets exactly 1 at any age.
regulars.tenureNote: Time constant of the regular base: 1 - exp(-months / 6) is 63% after six months and 86% after a year. D06: month one sells a third of month six; one vendor's data: 38.2% of cafe customers come back within six months (https://www.restolabs.com/blog/cafe-industry-statistics).
regulars.liftNote: Demand added (or lost) at the best (worst) shop on a block where every guest could become a regular. D06: 30% of first visits become regulars at average quality, 20% to 45% with quality: the stock of regulars moves between x0.67 and x1.5, and regulars are about 60% of orders. Most of that is already in the engine's quality and reputation terms (exp(0.93 x 0.2 + 0.74 x 0.2) = +40% for quality and reputation 0.7), so only 0.2 is left for the stock itself. qualitySpan: the lift is full when quality and reputation are both 0.2 away from 0.5. My estimates.
regulars.priceStepNote: D06 price_memory: a rise of up to 4% within a month costs only the ordinary elasticity; 4% is the yearly drift of menu prices (Toast: median drip coffee +4.3% in the year to February 2026). https://pos.toasttab.com/blog/data/toast-restaurant-trends-report-coffee-prices-2026
regulars.priceLossNote: Share of regulars who leave per point of monthly price rise above the free step. D06: a price step costs about 3% of demand for two months. A 15% rise is 11 points over: 0.11 x 0.5 = 5.5% of regulars, x 0.55 (regulars' share on a residential block) = 3% of demand in the month of the rise, half of it in the next month, nothing after. Check against Starbucks North America, second fiscal quarter of 2025: about 3% higher prices, transactions -4%.
regulars.closureNote: Share of regulars lost per day closed by an inspection. My estimate: a regular comes about three times a week (D06: two to four), so 43% of them meet a closed door on a given day; I assume 7% of those do not come back: 0.43 x 0.07 = 0.03. The loss fades in a straight line over three months.
regulars.steadyShareNote: D06: at steady state regulars give 55-65% of orders; Square case study: 65-70% of revenue from repeat customers at one roastery. Used as a check for the kpi on a residential block, not as an input.

profiles.name: Takeaway counter
profiles.pitch: A short counter, a fast line, a low price. Lives on the morning rush.
profiles.risk: A thin bar at 8 am: the line walks. Guests who want a seat leave or take it to go. On an office block weekends and August are empty.
profiles.note: Eight window stools. $8.00 sits between the D06 commuter ticket of $6.50 and the pack's $8.50: with the engine's fixed cost of goods per order ($2.21) a lower price does not pay on any door of the map. Four people on payroll put three at the bar in the rush with the owner: 77 orders an hour. Earns most where a bigger room does not fit: doors under about 600 sq ft.

profiles.name: Neighborhood cafe with seats
profiles.pitch: A room people stay in. Earns on regulars, loses when the tables are held all afternoon.
profiles.risk: Regulars remember last month's price; a closed door after an inspection sends them to the neighbor.
profiles.note: The pack's reference shop with six more seats: 24 seats need 395 + 24 x 18 = 827 sq ft and a customer restroom (20 seats or more, Health Code 81.22).

profiles.name: Specialty coffee bar
profiles.pitch: Better beans, better machine, a higher price. Needs guests who choose by quality.
profiles.risk: Students and commuters will not pay $10; without tourists or a prime block the room stays half empty.
profiles.source: packs/parts/cafe/D06-demand.json (guestSegments: tourist ticket $12), packs/cafe.json (kits.premium, levers.sourcing, levers.staff_pay)
profiles.note: $10 sits under the D06 tourist ticket of $12 and at 1.03 of the fair price for quality 0.73 ($9.67), inside what the engine forgives (1.15). Quality target: premium kit +0.11, specialty sourcing +0.05, pay above market +0.04, shift lead +0.03 and its own share: about 0.73. The bar is slower (staffing.leverSpeed).

extra.profilesNote: Starting sets, not buttons: every field is an ordinary player decision (kit, seats, price, team, levers). 'staff' is the team for a door with about 250 orders a day; on a busier door the owner adds baristas (build/FORMATS.md, section 7). Which profile earns most on which door: node packs/parts/cafe/D20-examples.mjs, sections C and H.
